articles.title: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
articles.context: Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 47 (2026)
articles.context: The Bad | Autonomous AI-Powered Pentesting Tool “ARTEX” Abused to Launch Global Cyberattacks A FLASH advisory from the FBI went out this past week, warning that threat actors...
articles.full_text:
The Good | Italian Officials Extradite “8-Digits” Ransomware Affiliate & U.S. Courts Sentence SMS Attacker to Prison

Italian authorities have extradited a Kazakh national, Roman Khlynovskiy, to the United States to face charges for orchestrating attacks against the American healthcare and education sectors. Prosecutors allege that Khlynovskiy operated within the "8-Digits Team", an affiliate syndicate linked to INC and Lynx ransomware operations.

The group breached networks across six states, stealing over 50 terabytes of sensitive data, including 70 million medical files, to extort over $500 million in ransom demands. Khlynovskiy now faces up to 27 years in prison on multiple cyber fraud and extortion counts if convicted.

U.S. federal courts also sentenced 24-year-old Tyler Robert Buchanan to six years in prison for the theft of millions in cryptocurrency through multiple breaches. In custody since April 2025, Buchanan pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Buchanan and his conspirators targeted corporate employees across technology, telecommunications, and outsourcing firms through hundreds of SMS phishing messages. After tricking staff into giving up enterprise credentials, they executed SIM-swapping attacks to compromise cryptocurrency accounts, ultimately stealing over $11.6 million in digital assets before federal investigators dismantled the ring.

In Ukraine, police partnered with the FBI to arrest four members of an international ransomware group linked to over $40.5 million in ransom payments. The criminal network breached at least 28 corporate victims across logistics, energy, finance, and healthcare sectors worldwide.

To infiltrate corporate networks, the attackers deployed social engineering tactics combined with AI-generated voice calls to impersonate IT support specialists and steal network credentials. Law enforcement officers conducted 66 coordinated searches across 11 regions, seizing computers, mobile phones, bank cards, and nearly $370,000 in cash.

The Bad | Autonomous AI-Powered Pentesting Tool “ARTEX” Abused to Launch Global Cyberattacks

A FLASH advisory from the FBI went out this past week, warning that threat actors are deploying an AI-powered pentesting framework called ARTEX to automate cyberattacks across global organizations. Written in the Go programming language, ARTEX operates as an automated penetration testing suite that translates high-level attacker objectives into coordinated tasks executed by specialized software agents.

Rather than deploying its own machine-learning models, the framework integrates directly with commercial LLMs, including OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, DeepSeek, Grok, and others. These autonomous agents perform reconnaissance, discover software vulnerabilities, execute exploits, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data with minimal human supervision.

The FBI highlighted how ARTEX accelerates attack velocity, compressing intrusion timelines from initial targeting to privileged access to under three hours in multiple cases. The framework proves particularly effective at identifying overlooked perimeter weaknesses, such as exposed partner portals, unpatched legacy services, and misconfigured third-party application programming interfaces.

Although the original developer, Autumn-27, removed the primary GitHub repository in October, threat actors continue to distribute the software through community forks, archived mirrors, and a commercial edition dubbed “ARTEX PRO”.

The FBI report notes several high-profile intrusions driven by the toolset, including the October ConnectWise supply-chain breach by China-aligned group Storm-0940, which attempted unauthorized authentication across more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer tenants.

Chinese-speaking operators have also been observed pairing ARTEX with Claude Code to breach major South Korean financial institutions, while one espionage-focused actor targeted over 200 organizations across 14 countries.

SentinelOne customers are protected from ARTEX agents via Behavioral AI, which detects the shell spawned by a compromised web application and the reconnaissance tools the ARTEX agent runs, the escalation to root on a Linux host, and DLL sideloading on a Windows host.

The Ugly | Attackers Target Critical “Java4Shell” Flaw in OpenJDK Across Enterprise Applications

A critical memory corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK, dubbed “Java4Shell”, enables unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute arbitrary code in popular enterprise software, including Atlassian Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, JFrog Artifactory, and Keycloak. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938 with a CVSS score of 9.2, the flaw resides within the hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding routine of the HotSpot Java Virtual Machine.

The issue impacts OpenJDK 17.0.6 onward, including versions 21, 25, and 27. However, exploitation strictly requires x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions. Since Java applications decode Base64 data in authentication headers, tokens, and file uploads before authenticating users, remote adversaries can trigger the flaw without credentials.

A malformed Base64 string ending with an extraneous equals sign forces the decoder to write 62 fixed bytes past buffer boundaries. In controlled testing, researchers chained this overflow to expand adjacent memory arrays, reading server secrets via a technique called “JavaBleed” and redirecting program flow to achieve complete remote code execution (RCE).

The bug lacks a universal exploit payload. Instead, each target requires customized memory arrangement and precise timing. Researchers independently rediscovered the flaw in an hour using an AI coding agent and built a first working exploit two hours later; an earlier public bug report from June had gone unpatched.

While Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, threat actors have begun probing internet-facing infrastructure. Honeypots have logged reconnaissance traffic and blind exploitation attempts, though no successful in-the-wild exploitation has been confirmed.

CISA has also issued an advisory urging immediate patching. SentinelOne customers are protected against Java4Shell. SentinelOne continues to defend its customers against Java4Shell, with details found here.

articles.title: The New Analyst Learning Curve: Training and Retaining Talent in the Autonomous SOC
articles.context: Give each analyst a yearly rotation through incident response, threat hunting, or detection engineering
articles.full_text:
Ask a senior analyst how they learned the job, and closing false positives rarely comes up. That work mostly built alert fatigue. The learning happened in rarer moments: the real hit, the escalation that became an incident, the Tier 2 analyst walking you through what you missed.

Agentic investigation now clears much of that queue. For coverage, that's a clear win. For your bench, it removes the place where people learned. Earlier this year, we mapped where the analyst role is heading. This blog covers the leader's side: how to get your people there without losing what the queue used to teach.

Security comes from habits repeated in everyday moments. Analyst judgment is built the same way, through reps. Naturally, if AI removes those reps, leaders have to schedule the practice back in.

The Autonomous SOC can relieve the grind that drives burnout, but only for leaders who deliberately maintain the learning that used to happen naturally. The grind was also the learning curve, and organizations must prove it that they haven’t lost it.

Two Talent Problems, One Shift

By taking over triage, AI now affects retention and the talent pipeline at once, and each problem feeds the other.

Start with retention: in addition to shift work, after-hours pages, understaffing, and pay, repetitive work has driven SOC attrition for years. AI is supposed to relieve that repetition, but the early data is mixed: in ISC2's 2026 Rethinking AI's Impact on Cybersecurity Roles report, 48% of professionals using AI say it lowered their stress, while 32% say it raised it. That second group is more likely to report spending extra time validating AI output and deciding when to trust it. Without structure, AI moves the stress into validation work.

The pipeline shows a similar split: the same report found 56% say AI has reduced the need for entry-level roles, while 53% say it is creating new entry-level opportunities. Both can be true: the old entry-level job is shrinking and a different one is taking its place. And AI skills now top the list of skills needs in ISC2's 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, cited by 41% of respondents who reported a skills need. You can't hire your way out of a senior shortage if no one is coming up the ladder behind them.

The obvious objection: if AI handles triage, juniors don't need to learn it. ISC2's respondents disagree: 62% say AI has not reduced the need for foundational skills, versus 26% who say it has. Someone still has to recognize a wrong verdict, and that judgment used to come from triage.

The Capabilities At Risk

Reviewing an investigation is a different skill from conducting one. An analyst can become very good at evaluating an automated system's work without the independent expertise to see when that system is fundamentally wrong. The capabilities most at risk are the ones the old queue exercised without anyone planning it:

Approaching an unfamiliar problem with no verdict to start from

Forming competing hypotheses instead of testing the first one offered

Noticing missing or incomplete evidence

Recognizing when the premise of an investigation is wrong

Write these down. Every practice below should build at least one of them, and every metric should test whether they hold.

What the Job Is Now

Responsibilities are shifting at every level of the SOC.

Tier 1 analysts move from closing every alert to reviewing AI verdicts and escalating the ones that don't hold up.

Natural-language querying speeds up hunting, but writing and reading queries is how they learn the data: the schema, the parsing gaps, the missing logs.

The path out of triage runs toward detection engineering, where analysts write and tune the logic the AI depends on.

Workflow design and leadership reporting stay with SOC engineering, IR leads, and managers, who now also own the rules the AI works within.

Each new responsibility assumes judgment that analysts used to build by doing the old one. Training must supply it now.

Training: Rebuilding the Learning Curve

Training is also how autonomy gets earned, as we covered in our retrospective review of our Autonomous SOC Maturity Model. Partial Autonomy (Level 3) is built on how analysts conduct investigations independently, and how they review investigations: which AI results they accept, modify, or override. Trained analysts make their records trustworthy before the system acts alone.

Five practices a SOC manager can start this quarter:

Run blind investigations. Have analysts work a share of live alerts cold, before they see the AI's verdict. Replay past incidents the same way, with the verdict withheld. Then use the AI's evidence chain as the answer key. Additionally, expand peer reviews: Add in 5 to 10 AI-closed cases per analyst per week and run quality assurance. This keeps investigative skills sharp and teaches where AI is reliable and where it needs a human.

Schedule the reps. Purple teaming, atomic tests, replays of past incidents, and tabletop exercises put analysts in front of attacks where the answer is known. Put them on a fixed calendar so they survive a busy quarter. Emulated attacks also let you score what the AI missed and what the analysts missed, separately. Current threat intelligence keeps the techniques realistic.

Make the AI's work the curriculum. Have juniors trace agentic investigations back to the raw telemetry: what was gathered, what was compared, why the conclusion followed. In addition, review the misses: wrong verdicts expose exactly where the AI's reasoning broke. Ask why the AI missed and feed the answer back into your workflows.

Treat ownership as governance training. Stage people the way you stage automation: crawl, walk, run. Juniors start by reviewing verdicts, then own a low-risk automated workflow such as phishing response. From there, they expand by domain. Ensure they read generated queries, because they’re learning AI verifiability and governance.

Train analysts. Give each analyst a yearly rotation through incident response, threat hunting, or detection engineering. Teams without those functions in-house can co-investigate with an MDR or IR partner.

Retaining: Make the New Work Visible and Rewarded

Training without recognition just builds a better resume for your competitor.

Rewrite the career ladder. If promotion criteria still count alerts closed, you're rewarding work that AI now does. Promote on independent investigation performance, as well as hypotheses tested, AI misses caught, and detection coverage added.

Change what you measure. Measure independent detection rate on emulated attacks, and pair it with a rubric that measures blind investigation quality. In addition, run unassisted exercises on novel attack scenarios twice a year.

Protect the time you free up. If saved capacity is immediately backfilled with more queue work, you get the same burnout with better tools.

Give real governance authority. Analysts who set the boundaries the AI works within have a stake in the system, and that ownership is a reason to stay.

Training for the Work That's Here Now

In the Autonomous SOC Maturity Model, Partial Autonomy (Level 3) is where the work is now. Human oversight is moving from reviewing individual actions to governing a system's behavior within a defined scope. However, training programs can produce good-looking metrics while independent skill erodes for years.

As such, the idea of verifiability is more important than ever. Purple AI, for example, shows the evidence chain behind every verdict, so you can grade analysts against it, test it against emulated attacks, and see where each falls short.

Two questions belong on every security leader’s agenda:

Which capabilities are we preserving?

How do we test that analysts can perform independently?

We believe that expansion from Partial Autonomy (Level 3) to High Autonomy (Level 4) should occur only when independent human capability is shown to hold. Governance precedes autonomy, and proven human skill is part of that governance.

articles.title: LABScon26 Replay | Governing Just-in-Time Intelligence: AI, Dual-Use Capabilities, and the Limits of Guardrails
articles.context: For policymakers, AI providers and threat researchers, this talk offers a historical lens on how offensive capability spreads and a starting point for thinking about how to...
articles.full_text:
In his LABScon 26 talk, Mauro Vignati, Advisor on Digital Technologies of Warfare at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), argues that guardrails cannot address the deeper problem with frontier AI. Advanced cognitive capabilities are now distributed through the same on-demand, as-a-service model that has shaped industry, and later cybercrime, for seventy years. That model was designed for industrial efficiency, not for technology this powerful.

Vignati traces the model back to Toyota’s post-war just-in-time production system, built on the principle that customers get only what they need and pay only for what they get. The IT needed to coordinate that system helped give rise to application service providers and eventually to software-as-a-service. Cybercriminals later adopted the same logic for crimeware and ransomware, and hacktivists for DDoS campaigns. In each case the people taking part needed no technical skill of their own.

Model-as-a-service differs from its predecessors because the capability is dual-use at the source, supplied by private technology firms largely independent of who the end users are or what they intend. Vignati explains why criminals who tried to build their own AI systems have largely turned to wrapping commercial ones instead, leaving the legitimate economy to carry the cost of training and infrastructure. He then draws on cybernetics’ law of requisite variety, the principle that any system regulating another must match its complexity, to argue that AI governance has no simple fix. In its place he proposes a layered framework for deciding what a model can do, for whom and under what conditions.

His warning is that as long as the industry keeps offering powerful general-purpose models, criminals and activists will continue to parasitise commercial services.

For policymakers, AI providers and threat researchers, this talk offers a historical lens on how offensive capability spreads and a starting point for thinking about how to govern it.

About the Author

Mauro Vignati is Advisor on Digital Technologies of Warfare at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). His work focuses on the militarisation of digital space and AI, the exploitation of the cognitive domain as a means of confrontation, and the impact of digital technologies in armed conflict on civilians, critical infrastructure and society. He has more than 20 years of experience in cybersecurity and previously spoke at LABScon 2022.

About LABScon

This presentation was featured live at LABScon 2026, an immersive 3-day conference bringing together the world’s top cybersecurity minds, hosted by SentinelOne’s research arm, SentinelLABS.

articles.title: Black Friday Phishing Is Already Up 103%, and the Sale Hasn’t Started
articles.context: Scam detections in KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security were about four times higher in the first week of November than in the third week of October
articles.full_text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R, Jeewan Singh Jalal

You've been saving for that watch for months.

Or perhaps you have your eyes on a long-sought-after bag you keep returning to online, or a gift for someone you want to surprise this year.

An email arrives: "[Black Friday Early Access] Luxury Products starting from $$$." The brand looks familiar. The price is far lower than you have ever seen. And the email says you are among the first to know.

Would you click?

Most people would at least look, and that is what the sender is counting on. There is no attachment and no urgent warning, only a short pitch, a brand you trust and one click. Attackers do not need to break into anything. They only need you to want a deal.

KnowBe4 Threat Lab researchers tracked this pattern from August to early November 2026. Read on for how fast it grew, which sectors received it, how one early access campaign works from email to checkout, and what to do before you click.

Key Findings

Volume climbed well before the sale. KnowBe4 Defend saw Black Friday scam detections build from the third week of October and rise 260% in the first week of November over the week before.

The targets were not mainly retailers. Industrial and Infrastructure organizations made up the largest share (25%), followed by Public Sector, Education, and Nonprofit (21.2%). Retail and Consumer came third at 14.4%.

Brand names did the work. The sender name showed a well-known luxury brand, while the email address belonged to an unrelated domain.

Redirects hide the destination. The button passed victims through intermediate websites before landing on the fake store, which can help a message slip past email gateways.

The store was built to look legitimate. It used steep discounts, authenticity and warranty claims, free worldwide shipping, a human verification Captcha, and payment through Paypal.

The end goal was personal and payment data. Checkout pages collected personal information and payment details, which leads to financial loss.

Why Are Attackers Starting Before the Sale Does?

Few events draw as much shopper attention as Black Friday. You expect sale emails, you look for big discounts, and you are ready to buy fast. Attackers time their messages to that calendar and place them next to real offers in your inbox.

The timing also helps them. Many real retailers now run "early access" events weeks before Black Friday, so an early access email feels normal even when no sale exists.

How Fast Did Early Black Friday Scam Volume Grow?

KnowBe4 Defend saw Black Friday scam detections rise 260% in the first week of November over the week before. Detections were a handful across August and September, began to build in the third week of October and reached their highest week so far in the first week of November, with the busiest days on the Tuesday and the Sunday of that week.

Volume gives attackers extra cover. Scam emails arrive in the same flood as ordinary retailer marketing, with the same sale subject lines, the same brand names, and the same kind of offers. Little sets them apart at a glance, so a fake offer is easy to overlook.

The PhishER Plus measure points the same way: Black Friday and holiday-sale emails were 103% higher in October than September and 165% higher in the first week of November. Against an August and September baseline, they ran about double across October and about eight times higher in the first week of November. Scam detections in KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security were about four times higher in the first week of November than in the third week of October.

Which Sectors Received These Emails?

These scams are not aimed at retailers alone. Industrial and Infrastructure organizations made up the largest share at 25%, followed by Public Sector, Education, and Nonprofit at 21.2%. Retail and Consumer organizations made up only 14.4%.

The spread shows that a sale email does not need to match your job to reach you. People in factories, government offices, and schools shop online like everyone else, and many do it from work devices and work inboxes. A scam that lands there puts your employer at risk, not only your wallet.

What Does an Early Access Lure Look Like?

KnowBe4 Threat Lab is tracking a phishing campaign that sends "early access" emails pointing to fake luxury stores. Luxury goods were the dominant lure theme. Of the scam emails in the campaigns we reviewed, about 94% were luxury goods: watches made up 43%, bags and leather goods 28%, and Louis Vuitton handbags 23%. The campaign runs in three steps.

1. The email

The sender name shows a well-known brand, but the email address belongs to an unrelated domain. The message is short: a brand, an offer, and a button.

Louis Vuitton was the only brand named in the subject lines. The other lures named no brand, only a product type such as luxury watches or leather bags.

2. The redirect

The button does not go straight to the store. It sends the victim through redirect links on other websites before the final page, which hides the destination from the reader and can help the message get past email gateways.

3. The store and the checkout

The final page is a polished online store. It lists unrealistic discounts and promises authenticity, warranties, and free worldwide shipping. At checkout it asks for personal information and payment details.

Every step feels routine. By the end, the attackers hold your personal information and your payment details.

How Does the Attack Unfold From Start to Finish?

The diagram below puts the whole chain in one view. It begins with the surge in campaign emails, moves through a branded lure and an unrealistic offer, and ends in financial loss once a victim enters personal information and payment details at checkout.

Why Do These Emails Work?

They work because they speak to how people decide, not because they use advanced technology.

A price that looks like a rare find. An unrealistic deal that makes the deal feel like luck.

Fear of missing out. "Early access" pushes the reader to act before other shoppers do.

Borrowed credibility. Well-known brand names and perfect impersonation make the store look real.

Each detail seems small. Together, they make you less likely to stop and question the offer.

What Should You Do Before You Click?

You can break the chain at the lure, the offer, or the checkout page, before any money moves.

Type the retailer's address yourself. Do not use the link in the email.

Check the sender's address against the brand it claims to be. A familiar display name proves nothing.

Treat a price far below normal as a warning, not a bargain.

Do not treat a payment logo as proof. A PayPal logo on a page does not make the sale legitimate.

Report the email to your security team and enter no details.

Already shared your details? Call your bank or card issuer as soon as possible to block the card and dispute the transaction.

What can security teams do?

Run phishing simulations and training before peak shopping periods, using lures such as early access offers and deep discounts.

Make reporting easy, and review reported messages quickly during the weeks before Black Friday, when volume is highest.

Remind employees that these early sales scam emails reach work inboxes too, and that the same checks apply.

Where Can KnowBe4 Help?

This campaign relies on trust: a familiar brand, an "early access" offer and a short, clean pitch. That is the layer KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security is designed to secure.

KnowBe4 Defend: Real-Time Behavioral AI

In this campaign, the harmful step comes after the click, when redirect links carry the victim to a fake store. Defend does not wait for a payload to appear.

Behavioral AI and natural language processing analyze inbound mail flow for the signals that give social engineering away: urgency, mismatched context, and a message that does not fit how the sender normally behaves. A well-known luxury brand name sent from an unrelated domain is one example.

These checks do not depend on file signatures or known-bad domains.

Context-Aware Warning Banners

Defend adds a warning banner directly into the email, so the user sees the alert before deciding whether to act. In this campaign, that moment comes before the click on the offer and before the checkout page asks for personal information and payment details.

PhishER Plus

Effective security needs both automated detection and users who report what they see. PhishER Plus gives employees a simple way to flag suspicious email and gives security teams a central dashboard to triage reports. With capabilities such as Global Blocklist, Global PhishRIP and automated quarantine workflows, security operations can act quickly on user-reported risk.

Security Awareness Training

KnowBe4 Security Awareness Training provides regular simulated phishing and training modules that help users spot common red flags: unrealistically low prices, sender domains that do not match the brand, and suspicious links. Running these simulations before peak shopping periods prepares your workforce for offers like this one.

articles.title: Russian Espionage Actor Star Blizzard Focuses on Cloud Identities for Mass Data Theft
articles.context: The latest analysis, based on two recent intrusions at US-based organizations, provides new details into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft, which...
articles.full_text:
New analysis from Google has revealed how Russian cyber-espionage group Star Blizzard is using sophisticated social engineering techniques and cloud account compromises to collect intelligence from targets across North America and Europe.

The group, also known as Coldriver, Callisto, Cold Relic and Gossamer Bear, is known for its use of spearphishing techniques to steal credentials from high-value targets in sectors related to policy making and defense.

Once Cold Relic compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets.

The latest analysis, based on two recent intrusions at US-based organizations, provides new details into the group’s social engineering and post-compromise tradecraft, which includes a growing focus on cloud compromise for data collection and to help facilitate attacks on other organizations.

“Cold Relic’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners,” Google wrote in a blog dated November 17, 2026.

“Their ability to navigate across multiple cloud ecosystems highlights that organizations must defend their entire identity estate holistically,” the researchers added.

Google has also observed evidence of new phishing operations by the threat actor as recently as November 2026, showing that the group remains an active threat.

Read now: Microsoft and US Government Disrupt Russian Star Blizzard Operations

The Latest Cold Relic Techniques

The first intrusion tracked by Google took place in late 2025, when Star Blizzard compromised the cloud productivity environment of a US-based organization.

The threat actor leveraged a residential proxy network in the US located in close geographical proximity to the victim. It used the stolen credentials of a super admin account in combination with a multi-factor authentication (MFA) push notification fatigue attack to gain access.

After the victim user accepted an MFA request, Star Blizzard used its super admin privileges to download the contents of the entire organization’s cloud storage drive by both mass sharing files to an attacker-operated email account and downloading files directly.

It also exported full employee lists and initiated a domain-wide data export via Google Workspace Customer Takeout via the stolen credentials.

Additionally, the actor took steps to remove forensic evidence of its activity, including deleting Alert Center notifications.

Following this activity, Star Blizzard was found to have maintained access to the victim’s environment for several months, continuing to target cloud drive document access related to credentials, email archives, personnel information and other documents related to its intelligence collection aims.

When the actor was removed from the victim’s environment, Google said it observed email accounts used to impersonate employees from the victim organizations to target individuals in the same professional circles.

The second intrusion tracked by the Google researchers arose from Star Blizzard impersonating an employee from the first compromise. The actor initiated communications over a secure messaging app, ultimately sharing phishing links during the course of the conversation.

These links successfully provided the actor with credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID, which was used by the second victim as its federated single sign-on provider (SSO) for Google Workspace.

Upon successful authentication, Star Blizzard registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion.

As in the first case, the group performed bulk download of files accessible in the compromised user’s cloud drive.

Google’s analysis of the two incidents noted that in addition to the mass collection of files and email archives, Star Blizzard undertakes searches for data that can support subsequent spear-phishing operations, including organizational rosters, contact lists, resumes, and event schedules to build convincing pretexts for future targets.

Organizations Urged to Harden Systems Against Cold Relic Activity

Google set out a range of recommendations for security teams to mitigate the updated tactics deployed by Star Blizzard. These include:

Given Cold Relic’s use of residential proxy networks, organizations should enrich authentication logs with residential proxy and VPN IP reputation feeds and apply conditional access policies to block or detect logons from known proxy networks

Implement cloud storage data loss prevention (DLP) policies to warn or block users attempting to create, upload, or externally share files matching sensitive patterns. This is because Cold Relic’s intrusions were helped by users storing credentials and other secrets within their organization’s cloud storage platforms

If an intrusion is identified, revoke all user sessions and force password resets for impacted accounts

Enforce phishing-resistant MFA, particularly hardware keys which cannot be intercepted or approved via fatigue attacks

Restrict and audit passkey registrations

On November 17, 2026, security researchers at Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS 4.0: 9.2 Critical), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder that allows malformed Base64 input to trigger remote code execution (RCE).

Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution in default configurations of Apache Kafka Broker, Atlassian Confluence and Jira, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, Keycloak, Gerrit, PingFederate, and Spring Boot applications, and post-authentication execution against Elasticsearch.

Oracle released patches addressing this flaw in its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update. Organizations running OpenJDK 17.0.6 or newer on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI support are affected. Additionally, affected Oracle Java SE versions include 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, and 27.0.1.0.3.

What Is Java4Shell

The flaw sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application. Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.

Recommended Next Steps

Inventory every Java runtime. Record the vendor, full build version, OS, CPU architecture, and owner across your environment—including containers, bundled installations, and vendor appliances. Prioritize internet-facing applications, authentication services, and business-critical systems.

Mitigate immediately by disabling AVX-512 (if unable to patch right away). Start x86-64 JVMs with the flag -XX:UseAVX=2. Note: Apply this flag on x86-64 hosts only; ARM JVMs do not recognize it and will fail to start.

Apply Oracle’s security updates once available. Monitor Oracle and your specific OpenJDK distribution vendor for patched builds addressing CVE-2026-114938, and upgrade affected runtimes as soon as fixes are released. For products that bundle their own Java runtime, follow the vendor’s supported update path.

Hunt and audit logs. Where your WAF, reverse proxy, or application logs capture Base64 values (HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens), inspect them after normal application parsing, and flag any that meet all of the following conditions:

Total length L (including padding) is 65 or more

$L \pmod{64}$ is 1, 2, or 3

Ends with one or two = characters (not exceeding $L \pmod{64}$)

All other bytes belong to the standard Base64 alphabet

SentinelOne’s Defense Against Java4Shell

The exploit arrives as a malformed Base64 string that corrupts memory inside the running JVM, so there is no file to scan at that stage. Instead of relying on CVE-specific signatures, SentinelOne protects against what an attacker does next.

Real-Time Behavioral & Static Protection

Across both Windows and Linux, the SentinelOne Agent’s behavioral engines continuously monitor JVM-hosted services and web servers in real time to detect malicious post-exploitation activity – regardless of the initial exploit vector. If an attacker achieves RCE and acts on the host, the Agent monitors for common post-exploitation behaviors, including a JVM process spawning a shell to run a remote or obfuscated one-liner (such as downloading a payload and piping it to a shell), suspicious child processes, credential access, persistence, and payload execution. Files written to disk during an attack, including JSP web shells and second-stage binaries, are evaluated by the Agent’s static engines across both operating systems.

Linux: In addition to general JVM behavioral monitoring, the Linux Agent applies deeper behavioral checks across web and application servers. These monitor for web shell drops, server-initiated file-transfer utilities, user enumeration, access to sensitive credential stores (such as shadow files and SSH keys), password changes, and use of AWS IMDS tokens– a common indicator of cloud credential theft following exploitation.

Windows: Alongside JVM and post-exploitation behavioral monitoring (such as suspicious child processes, credential access, and persistence), the Windows Agent specifically monitors web server processes for spawning suspicious child-processes as well as unauthorized file drops and execution.

Customers across all OS platforms with Live Security Updates enabled benefit from our most up to date detection capabilities.

Platform Detection Rules

For an added layer of visibility on top of Agent telemetry, SentinelOne provides Platform Detection Rules that can alert on post-exploitation activity from Java application servers and general Java-based exploitation. SentinelOne customers have access to these rules and can enable them today.

Threat Hunting

Our Wayfinder Threat Hunting teams provide an additional 24/7 layer of protection using AI-powered hunting systems that continuously look for post-exploit activity, persistence, and lateral movement across web servers and other potentially vulnerable applications. They add human review and agentic technology to find attacker activity that may originate from this or other application vulnerabilities.

articles.title: Scans for LiteLLM/Starlette (CVE-2026-42271, CVE-2026-48710), (Mon, Nov 16th)
articles.context: Looks like our attacker attempts to play with characters like '[', maybe to evade some of the filters built around the PoC exploits
articles.full_text:
This weekend, we started seeing requests for /mcp-rest/test/tools/list hitting our honeypots. These requests appear to attempt to exploit CVE-2026-42271 and CVE-2026-48710. Horizon3.ai published a short write-up about how these vulnerabilities can be chained to achieve remote code execution without authentication [Horizon3]

POST /mcp-rest/test/tools/list HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost] Content-Type: application/json Authorization: Bearer nothing Accept: */* Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, zstd User-Agent: Python/3.14 aiohttp/3.14.5 Content-Length: 74 {"server": {"transport": "stdio", "command": "id", "args": [], "env": {}}}

The problem starts with Starlette. Versions prior to 1.0.1 do not validate the "Host" header. This vulnerability became known as "BadHost". Starlette will take the unvalidated Host header and use it to build the complete URL. This URL is then used to make access control decisions. The class PoC exploit published uses characters like '/', '?,' and # in the Host header to confuse the access control logic. Looks like our attacker attempts to play with characters like '[', maybe to evade some of the filters built around the PoC exploits.

Here are the different "odd" Host headers I have seen so far:

localhost] [localhost 127.0.0.1] litellm.proxy

Starlette is a Python web framework, and if tools like LiteLLM rely on it for access control, exploits happen. For LiteLLM, this enables exploitation of the /mcp-rest/test/tools/list endpoint, which usually requires authentication.

A couple of lessons learned:

This isn't a new vulnerability, and exploitation has been reported back in July. But attackers keep exploiting existing vulnerabilities, modifying them to evade filters and find new victims.

When building WAF rules or similar filters, focus on the vulnerability, not on specific exploits. In this case, flag all characters that are not supposed to appear in a hostname, or, better yet, allow only specific hostnames.

If you write software, validate data components before assembling them into more complex entities. It is much easier to validate a hostname before combining it into a URL. Validating and constraining URLs is hard for "middleware" that must allow a wide range of URLs.

Reduce your attack surface. Aside from patching, this is probably the most important thing you can do right now to help you weather the current surge in new vulnerabilities.

[Horizon3] https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-42271-chained-with-cve-2026-48710/

-- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter|

articles.full_text:
Executive Summary

ARTEX is a Chinese open-source, AI-powered penetration testing platform designed to help security teams assess systems they own or are authorized to test. In recent weeks, it has been used in traditional cybercrime campaigns, including in attacks on South Korean banks. Although the original developer made ARTEX closed-source in mid-October, actively maintained forks and backups of the original repository remain publicly available to threat actors.

Nation-state actors swiftly adopted this new tool: a China-nexus espionage actor used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries. Another China-state aligned actor, who was responsible for the October 2026 ConnectWise supply chain compromise, used ARTEX to attempt mass sign-ins to more than 2,250 Azure tenants.

We assess with high confidence that ARTEX marks a change in the threat landscape: agentic offensive frameworks have moved from experiments to operational use by state-aligned and financially motivated actors alike. Since late August 2026, at least five actors and clusters have used ARTEX, from China-nexus espionage groups to a Cambodia-based criminal cluster. Closing the source in early October did not slow adoption.

The barrier to entry is low: Operators ran ARTEX in default configurations, and each campaign cost $145 to $1,500 in model time. The agents work at machine speed: in one case of suspected ARTEX use, an agent went from a leaked GitHub secret to Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. They can also be told to look for gaps, e.g. a Chinese-aligned actor told its agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor.

We expect more actors to adopt ARTEX and similar frameworks such as PentAGI and Cairn. For defenders, the time between a leaked secret or an exposed flaw and its exploitation can now be minutes, and IP blocklists lose value against agents that rotate through residential proxies. Rotating secrets, closing internet-facing flaws, and EDR coverage on every host now matter more than simply blocking indicators.

Key Highlights

A tool built for authorized testing now runs criminal campaigns. Across the 10 instances Check Point analyzed, operators used ARTEX exclusively for opportunistic, financially motivated cybercrime, mostly on a broad scale. The operators ran default configurations with default tools.

State-linked actors use it, too. For instance, a China-nexus espionage actor, used ARTEX against more than 200 organizations from October 17, 2026. Its operator told the agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor.

A supply chain compromise fed ARTEX more than 2,250 targets. Storm-0940 gained control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, including Cloud Backup, and used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants.

The agents ran without an operator. In multiple campaigns, nobody prompted the agents after the operator set the initial task goals.

The campaigns were cheap and the losses were real. Observed campaigns cost an estimated $700 to $1,500, recovering more than 300 signing certificates with their passwords or more than 190,000 Honor of Kings credentials, about 6,000 of them still valid, in exchange.

From GitHub to Key Vault in 5 minutes. In at least one case of suspected ARTEX use, an AI agent moved from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

What Is ARTEX

ARTEX is an agentic AI penetration testing platform that, by default, uses off-the-shelf tools like Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium, among others. Many operators routed their agents through residential proxies, and one operator built a custom skill for proxy use.

According to various reports, DeepSeek v4.1-flash was utilized as the primary model, with GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 used in additional Claude Code sessions. Models from the DeepSeek Flash family were the most prevalent across the 10 analyzed instances. Note that Operators configured American models on three instances and guardrails triggered only on Anthropic's Opus 5.5. As a consequence in this case, the actor then switched to more permissive Chinese models.

ARTEX at a Glance

Attribute

Detail

Name

ARTEX

Type

Agentic AI penetration testing platform

Origin

Chinese, open-source until October 8, 2026

Availability

Maintained forks and backups of the original repository, including ScopeWeaver and ARTEX PRO

Exposure

At least 2,500 systems hosting or having hosted ARTEX panels, 1,608 live and publicly available. 1,465 exposed consoles on November 3 and 4, 2026

Timeline

The following events list the most important milestones of this emerging threat:

Date (2026)

Event

August

Threat actors begin querying public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, suspected ARTEX use

September

Storm-0940 begins using ARTEX to automate attacks

October 7

Threat actors use ARTEX in attacks on South Korean banks

October 8

The developer makes ARTEX closed-source

Mid-October

Creation of new ARTEX C&C servers spikes, coinciding with prominent public reporting about the project

October 17

VAPOR PANDA begins ARTEX-enabled intrusions

October 19 to November 4

Storm-3358 actively using ARTEX

October 21

Microsoft attributes the supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant vendor application to Storm-0940

Exploitation in the Wild

Espionage and State-Linked Use

The China-nexus espionage actor VAPOR PANDA ran ARTEX-enabled intrusions for 11 days from October 17, 2026. The campaign targeted more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries, with post-exploitation confirmed at nine. Targets included foreign ministries, a European presidency, and US pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, and nuclear organizations. The operator told the agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor, judged from tasklist output and folder listings.

After access, the actor deployed BLOODALCHEMY through DLL sideloading by a renamed GameHook binary running as svchost.exe. CrowdStrike links the ARTEX controller to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure and distinguishes the campaign from Storm-0940.

Storm-0940, another China-state aligned actor, was responsible for the ConnectWise supply chain compromise. As early as September 2026, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to automate attacks, accelerate scanning and reconnaissance, and attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants.

Incident response engagements since late August 2026 found ARTEX in intrusions at US government, technology, chemicals, and manufacturing organizations. They found artex-probe files, numbered JSP web shells, and webhook.site callback URLs.

CERT-EU reports activity against EU institutions that "highly likely involved the use of ARTEX."

Criminal Campaigns

An analysis of three criminal campaigns using ARTEX found agents operated autonomously after initial goal-setting. These included Apple certificate theft across 10 signing shops, crypto-draining targeting payment infrastructure and TRON wallets, and harvesting over 190,000 gaming credentials. These operations demonstrated low financial barriers and high autonomy, with model costs ranging from $145 to $1,500.

State-linked actors and cybercriminals expanded usage beyond basic pentesting. For instance, VAPOR PANDA targeted over 200 organizations, Storm-0940 used access through a compromised vendor application to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, and Storm-3358 targeted Southeast Asian financial institutions, all using ARTEX.

Global intelligence advisories, including CERT-In and CERT-EU alerts, emphasize that agentic offensive tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, and Cairn represent a broader shift toward automated, machine-speed exploitation across both espionage and financial attacks.

Why This Matters

ARTEX now serves both espionage and financially motivated actors, enabling them to carry out their attacks at machine speed. The same framework ran intrusions against foreign ministries and defense organizations, sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 tenants, and criminal campaigns that stole signing certificates and gaming accounts. Seeing ARTEX in an intrusion no longer tells defenders who is behind it or what they want.

The skill and money needed to run a campaign have dropped. Operators ran ARTEX in default configurations, and each campaign cost $145 to $1,500 in model time. For less than $1,500, one operator came away with 3 validated signing certificates and their passwords, enough to sign apps that appear to come from the certificate owners.

Exposed weaknesses are found and used faster. The agents retry failed calls within seconds, and in one case of suspected ARTEX use, an agent got from a leaked GitHub secret to Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. A leaked key, an unauthenticated API, or an unpatched internet-facing application can now be found and exploited within minutes.

Trusted paths carry the risk further: one actor turned a compromised vendor application into a launch point against more than 2,250 tenants. One weak link at a vendor or in a delivery pipeline now exposes everyone downstream at machine speed.

Indicator-based defenses lose value against this kind of operator. The agents rotate through residential proxies, and one proxy service showed 79 exit IPs in 100 sampled identities. Behavior on the host and in the cloud stays the same when the addresses change, such as a web server that starts a shell or one app requesting tokens across several services. Coverage gaps are found just as fast: one actor told its agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor.

Attack Chain

The campaigns in this report show the breadth of TTPs that operators run through ARTEX, an agentic penetration testing framework. The same tool served web application exploitation, cloud identity abuse, a vendor supply chain compromise, and espionage implants.

Stage 1: Initial Access

Agents enter through whatever an internet-facing system exposes. In the described criminal campaigns, they used hardcoded administrator passwords, plaintext credential files in the web root, weak administrative credentials, and unauthenticated web APIs. They also exploited IDOR, command injection, and SSTI flaws. A Cambodia-based financially motivated cluster used anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery. A China-state aligned actor abused a compromised multitenant vendor application to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants. In the suspected ARTEX activity against cloud tenants, agents harvested secrets from public GitHub repositories.

Stage 2: Execution and Command and Control

Command injection and SSTI gave the agents code execution in web applications. Agents allegedly used a compromised OAuth application to run scripts on Azure VMs through Run Command against cloud tenants. The financially motivated cluster's agents used curl and netcat to fetch the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 remote access tools. In attacks against South Korean financial services, operators staged a JNDI/LDAP exploitation rig, and incident responders in other intrusions found numbered JSP web shells and webhook.site callbacks.

Stage 3: Escalation, Discovery, and Evasion

On a Linux host, an agent escalated from a low-privileged user to root through overly permissive folder access. Operator infrastructure also held exploit builds whose file names reference CVE-2022-2588 and CVE-2025-5054. A China-nexus espionage actor told its agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor, judged from tasklist output and folder listings. On the hosts it chose, it sideloaded the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor through a renamed GameHook binary running as svchost.exe. Operators routed agent traffic through residential proxies to rotate their source addresses.

Stage 4: Credential Harvesting

In the suspected ARTEX activity against cloud tenants, agents called Azure operations that return credentials, exfiltrated Key Vault data, and searched Azure DevOps for secrets. In one case, an agent went from a leaked GitHub secret to Key Vault data in five minutes. In AWS, agents searched CloudWatch logs with stolen long-term access keys and self-registered in public Cognito user pools. The criminal campaigns pulled AWS S3 keys from an unauthenticated API and found megabytes of plaintext credentials.

Stage 5: Collection and Monetization

In the suspected ARTEX activity against cloud tenants, agents downloaded SharePoint and OneDrive files and accessed mailbox items. The criminal agents collected more than 300 signing certificates with their passwords and about 6,000 valid gaming accounts, and wrote to an S3 bucket that served a crypto service's iOS apps.

Recommended Mitigations

Find and Rotate Exposed Secrets

Search public GitHub repositories and Azure DevOps for material the agents queried for, such as credentials, application secrets, and AI inference API keys. Rotate every secret you find.

Enable GitHub push protection so new secrets are blocked before they reach a repository.

Close Initial Access Paths

Audit web APIs for responses that return cloud credentials, such as the AWS S3 keys an unauthenticated API leaked in one campaign.

Disable anonymous file upload and fix server-side request forgery flaws on internet-facing systems.

Put administrative interfaces behind a VPN.

Limit the Blast Radius

Review which identities can read storage account keys, App Service settings and publishing credentials, connection strings, AI and ML connections and datastores, and AKS user credentials.

Restrict who can use Run Command on Azure VMs.

Restrict write access to S3 buckets that serve app manifests or landing pages.

Move applications to managed identities where possible, and set app management policies that restrict new secrets and credentials.

Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions.

Watch for Failed Attempts

Alert on Entra ID sign-in errors AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) and AADSTS7000222 (expired secret). Either one means someone holds a credential for your app. Treat a failure followed by a success as urgent.

Alert on one address authenticating to 3 or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across ARM, Key Vault, Storage, and Graph in a short window.

Alert on a failed API call that is retried shortly after with a different API version, such as the Key Vault rerun about 28 seconds after the first failure.

Alert on user agents that contain artex, the strings Datadog observed in AWS activity.

Block the Indicators

Block the IP addresses and domains in Observed Indicators (Appendix) at the firewall and proxy, and add the SHA-256 hashes to your endpoint blocklist. Treat the Tor exit node, VPN, and proxy addresses as hunting leads rather than blocks, because other traffic shares them. Investigate any historical connection to the indicators.

How SentinelOne Protects Customers

The SentinelOne® agent records what an ARTEX agent does once it reaches a managed host. Behavioral AI detects the shell spawned by a compromised web application, the reconnaissance tools it runs, the escalation to root on a Linux host, and DLL sideloading on a Windows host. Singularity™ AI SIEM correlates Entra ID sign-ins, Azure activity logs, and AWS CloudTrail with that endpoint activity to surface stolen service principal credentials and cloud keys in use. Each step is a hunting point in Purple AI®.

Correlate Identity and Cloud Activity in Singularity AI SIEM

Forward Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure activity logs, Microsoft 365 audit logs, AWS CloudTrail, and web server and WAF logs to Singularity AI SIEM. It ties a failed-then-successful service principal sign-in to the Key Vault, Storage, and Graph token requests the same app makes in a short window. Singularity Identity flags the Entra ID accounts and service principals the actors misuse.

Self-Hosted Customers Should Ensure Known Malicious Hashes Are Blocked

The hunts below find the same activity whatever the hash. Self-hosted customers without cloud reputation services should block every SHA-256 hash in Observed Indicators.

Hunt with Purple AI

Use Purple AI to hunt for the identity and cloud activity described in this report. In Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure activity logs, and AWS CloudTrail forwarded to Singularity AI SIEM, look for service principals that fail with an expired or invalid secret and then sign in successfully, one address signing in to many service principals, unexpected activity by vendor applications such as the affected ConnectWise apps, and requests with artex in the user agent. Look back to August 1, 2026, when the earliest reported activity began.

Use Purple AI to hunt on the endpoint for what an ARTEX agent does after it gets in. On hosts with an active agent, look for web server processes that start a shell, command lines and file paths that contain artx or artex, DLL sideloading by binaries posing as system processes, and connections to the addresses and domains in Observed Indicators. Treat each match as a lead to investigate, because authorized penetration testers also run ARTEX.

articles.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly in Cybersecurity - Week 46 (2026)
articles.context: The Bad | Turla Attackers Deploy Cereal Malware to Spy on Government Exchange Servers Russian state-backed threat group known as Turla is deploying a previously undocumented
articles.full_text:
The Good | Authorities Dismantle Crypto Scams, Ban Illicit Exchange & Seize Malware Infrastructure

Ukrainian law enforcement partnered with German authorities this week to dismantle a network of cryptocurrency scammers that stole over €4.3 million from victims in Europe. Operating out of Ukrainian centers, the criminals used social media and dating apps to carry out romance baiting and other schemes.

After building up trust, they coerced victims into depositing funds into bogus trading platforms and attacker-controlled cryptocurrency wallets. Coordinated raids across four regions yielded hardware wallets, computer equipment, SIM cards, and over $13,000 in seized currencies. The four detained suspects remain in pre-trial custody and face up to 12 years in prison.

In the U.S., the Department of the Treasury cut off MEXC Global cryptocurrency exchange from the American financial system over extensive sanctions evasion and ties to cybercrime gangs. Between 2021 and 2026, the global platform facilitated over $16 billion in illicit transactions, according to an enforcement order from U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

Regulators identified MEXC as a key financial clearinghouse for ransomware gangs, darknet activity, and state-backed entities evading sanctions across Russia, Iran, and North Korea. While FinCEN calls out deficiencies in the exchange’s anti-money laundering and customer verification policies, MEXC states they are reviewing the order with legal and compliance experts.

Europol and Eurojust also seized 257 domains and 235 servers powering the Gootloader, CastleRAT, and StealC malware operations. The joint takedown, part of the long-running Operation Endgame, spanned nine partner nations all targeting loaders, info-stealers, and remote access trojans (RATs) actively leveraged by cybercriminals to harvest corporate credentials and deploy secondary payloads.

Investigators uncovered over six million compromised credentials and $6.4 million victim datasets stored across the criminal infrastructure. Now, authorities are forwarding the recovered records to public breach-notification services to alert affected organizations and users.

The Bad | Turla Attackers Deploy Cereal Malware to Spy on Government Exchange Servers

Russian state-backed threat group known as Turla is deploying a previously undocumented .NET cyberespionage framework dubbed Cereal to intercept communications on Microsoft Exchange servers across government organizations. Researchers began tracking the first wave of attacks in 2025 when Tulra compromised a government body in Kazakhstan before striking a Romanian state agency. In Romania shortly after, operators configured the toolset to selectively capture sensitive email correspondence involving representatives from NATO and the European Union.

Turla (aka Snake, UNC4210), linked to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), engineered Cereal for stealthy, long-term intelligence gathering. The malware avoids external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure entirely. Instead, it abuses the compromised Exchange server itself as a centralized execution hub and persistent collection point. The framework comprises eight modular components that rely extensively on data serialization and in-memory execution to conceal illicit activity from security defenders.

A primary module, named CerealBox, injects directly into Exchange's transport service process, EdgeTransport.exe. Once inside, it hijacks existing transport handlers to inspect message traffic without registering unauthorized transport agents or interrupting normal email delivery. The module automatically compresses, encrypts, and stages messages containing PDF, DOC, or DOCX attachments matching targeted sender, recipient, or subject criteria.

At the same time, a passive backdoor named CerealNeuron listens for incoming encrypted web requests designed to blend with regular Exchange traffic. Upon receiving instructions, it launches disposable CerealRunner binaries that execute memory-resident payloads to query Active Directory, extract LSA secrets, inspect mailboxes, and return encrypted results to the backdoor for exfiltration.

Security analysts emphasize that Cereal's extensive concealment strategies reflect Turla’s deep understanding of .NET execution techniques running inside legitimate processes, marking a mature offensive platform ready for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage.

The Ugly | Threat Actors Breach Railway Infrastructure to Steal Customer AI Secrets

Cloud hosting platform Railway confirmed that threat actors exploited flaws within its build infrastructure to steal decrypted customer authentication secrets, resulting in an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized AI usage charges.

The intrusion began on October 20 when adversaries exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to escape build filesystem isolation and capture internal credentials. Using these credentials, the attackers accessed stored build histories and obtained a copy of Railway's monorepo source code to identify further exploitation paths across the environment.

The attackers then exploited an improperly configured OIDC trust binding within Railway's cloud deployment system, moving laterally to compromise an orchestration server. Since that machine managed fleet workloads, it held credentials authorized to decrypt customer environment variables via cloud key management services.

Between October 20 and October 21, the intrusion escalated into a 26-hour operational contest between Railway engineers and threat actors deploying autonomous AI agents to probe systems in parallel.

Forensic investigations revealed that the attackers specifically targeted environment variables containing API keys for major AI providers, likely seeking access for resale or model distillation. The breach potentially exposed credentials across at most 1.85% of workspaces, representing approximately 100,000 customer environments, alongside linked-account tokens for 1,852 users. However, forensic analysis showed no evidence that attackers accessed customer databases. The investigation also found no indication that attackers downloaded private Git repositories.

Railway fully evicted the threat actors on October 21, isolated each build within dedicated ephemeral virtual machines, and rotated affected tokens. While the company is coordinating with AI providers to secure customer refunds, it pledged to cover any fraudulent charges that vendors decline to reimburse.

Startups frequently work at a fast pace with lean teams wearing many hats. In many ways, Claude Tag (beta) is suited for how startups work. You @Claude to a Slack channel where your context lives, add connectors, and have your team assign and steer tasks together.

For startup teams new to using Claude Tag, one of the most frequent questions is “which channels should I add Claude to first?” To help answer it, we spoke with eight high growth startups to see how Claude Tag works inside their teams.

Featuring insights from

We heard from leaders at companies with visions from reinventing law firms to building the next generation of resource planning software. Some had added Claude to nearly every channel while others had focused deeply on one or two specific use cases.

The most common are contained in this guide, each with practical implementation details designed to help founders find and deploy the use cases that will move the needle for their team. Here are some examples of how the needle moved for the startups we spoke with:
